articles.title: Codex CLI installs a persistent, self-updating background daemon by default
articles.summary: Codex CLI installs a persistent, self-updating background daemon by default

top_comments: There aren't any documented settings to disable this, but there is a feature flag it currently sits behind. You can flip it in your ~/.codex/config.toml[1]: [features] daemon_auto_start = false There are also some files that it writes to in ~/.codex at startup: pid files, lock files, things like that. You can delete them and replace them with symlinks to /dev/null, then mark those unwritable with `chattr +i` or similar. Presumably then the background daemon will crash on startup, if the feature flag ever goes away.--1: https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/0c329ad2c9d5a2592128a1d...

Anthropic's recent policy update makes this abundantly clear:“When our products are used in ways that can affect someone's health, legal rights, finances, livelihood, or access to essential services, we require there to be a qualified ‘human in the loop’ (that is, someone who has the authority to review and, if necessary, change Claude’s recommendations), and for the individual affected to be told that AI was used.”Something as common as a family law case has the potential to affect all of the above. Now imagine being a petitioner, respondent, paralegal, or other 3rd party using Claude to review a draft document only to find out that Anthropic has sent your entire file to opposing counsel.It sounds egregious, but Anthropic is clearly stating they will use their own judgment to control what people can do with its product, and that they will treat customer data as if it's theirs to disseminate. articles.title: A Modern Web App in C
articles.summary: A Modern Web App in C

top_comments: My favorite trivia is that busybox has built-in cgi-bin support (and `rclone serve webdav` seems remiss to not mention as well). `https://elixir.bootlin.com/busybox/1.37.0/source/networking/...`Everything the post mentions is 100% true and well-reasoned, especially with the inclusion of pledge/chroot/etc. for dropping privileges.There's two diametrically opposed deployment mechanisms:1) stack towers of glop on top of each other until you're running a simple `echo "hello world"` on top of a docker container inside a vm in a proxmox server as part of a k8s cluster under a hypervisor running on remote compute...2) just run `bash -c 'echo "hello world"'` and front it with CGI (stateless, single binary, yada yada yada...)Take a peek at https://github.com/Domain/bash.cgi ... not that i'm suggesting that 'bash over busybox using cgi-bin' is the "proper architecture", it's more trying to illustrate that the amount of code that holds you back from being nearly truly "frameworkless" is tiny and easy to reason about.For some of the internal tooling I'm doing for work, I've been tending towards: some-cmd [--json|--markdown] ...yet-more-args... When you use the process and shell environment itself as a repl, you start trending towards `[--cgi-bin]` would "just" be another output type, and the ability (nay: foresight!) to ensure that your commands are independent, reproducible, and only depend on their input arguments leads you directly towards being runnable in both "hostile" (ie: firecracker vm / lambda-style) or very "comfortable" environments (ie: shell, debuggers, unit/integration tests).

An old version of binutils [1] explains what DDS means: How to encode VEX.vvvv: 0: VEX.vvvv must be 1111b. 1: VEX.NDS. Register-only source is encoded in VEX.vvvv where the content of source registers will be preserved. VEX.DDS. The second register operand is encoded in VEX.vvvv where the content of first source register will be overwritten by the result. VEX.NDD2. The second destination register operand is encoded in VEX.vvvv for instructions with 2 destination register operands. For assembler, there are no difference between VEX.NDS, VEX.DDS and VEX.NDD2. 2. VEX.NDD. Register destination is encoded in VEX.vvvv for instructions with 1 destination register operand. 3. VEX.LWP. Register destination is encoded in VEX.vvvv and one of the operands can access a memory location. [1] https://sourceware.org/git/?p=binutils-gdb.git;a=commitdiff;...

Similar to a comment I made a few hours ago. I find myself expressing a concern that something has been lost when people never interact with something directly.Most of the discussion today is about AI and how that causes this issue, but I have been though this experience a few times now.This instruction is essentially incomprehensible at a glance and requires a mental translation step to fillow. That doesn't affect it's use in a specific case, and compilers just use the instructions that they are programmed to use, so there isn't anything fundamentally wrong with this instruction or it's name other than the fact that it seems to be a key for a lock.If there were more people programming in asm, there would probably be enough minds interacting with the instructions to desire and have the capacity to design a better representation for the instruction set. I do believe that better designs at levels like that help solidify thinking in neighbouring levels. For instance with instruction representations, a better way to think about how the instruction is specified might reduce the cognitive load on chip designers and compiler writers.This kind of thing happens over and over when people move to new methods, there are artifacts that remain that are still useful in a modern context but only exist because they were designed at a time when the principles that underlying them were much more commonly used.Examples of this are music boxes and regular expressions, You can still find new instances for both, and they are good solutions for some tasks, but if anyone were to design something today to fill the niche of either, they would not come up with anything so enduring.It is easier to understand a music box than a regular expression finite automata, but both are wonders of design.It has occurred to me that this specific problem of ideas and methods left unconsidered may not be such a problem in an age of AI. It mY be that the capacity for AI to consider and link so many things that it will draw together elements from all of those domains to apply techniques that humans no longer focus upon onto issues that are currently relevant.I'm not sure if current AI is up to that particular task. It would be an interesting problem to set it.Design an assembler for a machine with a modern complex instruction set so that programming on assembler is a more mentally tractable task.It would be fascinating to see what such an open task would do to a model.

articles.title: Launch HN: Agent37 (YC F26) – Low-cost agent sandboxes for running agents
articles.summary: Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 (https://agent37.com). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox.You can view a video walkthrough of the product here: https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNoWe started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses.One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings.Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month.Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost:* When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost.* Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This alone was probably one of the biggest cost levers in reducing the cost.* Thirdly, you also want to pick a technology stack that lets you efficiently cache and share resources across the host. We use gVisor for better utilization and fast boot times. It lets us use available host memory across sandboxes without reserving a full VM’s memory for each one. There are tradeoffs: our gVisor sandboxes don’t support workloads like Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators.* And finally the size and shape of the hosts you buy also makes a big difference. RAM is typically the bottleneck when it comes to cost and not the CPU. This is specifically true for agent harness workloads, so when buying servers, we optimize for packing more RAM into a given host.We also host full VM sandboxes for workloads that need them, including running Docker at a slightly higher price, but they are still pretty low cost given the rest of the techniques.Overall, my learning has been that just by focusing on a niche of sandbox usecases, and optimizing for it you can give a much better cost/performance tradeoff.I was previously a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and an Engineering Manager at Quantcast. I built Amazon's internal AI chatbot, Diya, and their internal coding harness, Ziya.If you’re someone who’s looking to run agents on sandbox and are exploring a sandbox vendor, come check us out. We’re particularly looking for developers building messaging agents to try their workloads and challenge the limits and economics of our platform.Thanks!https://agent37.com

articles.title: Making big downloads resumable in Firefox
articles.summary: Making big downloads resumable in Firefox

top_comments: I'll try this.The way I have to resume downloads in Firefox is1. Move the .part file to a temp file2. Start the download again; a new .part file gets created3. Pause the download4. Move the temp file to the .part file, overwriting it5. Unpause the download; it resumes from where the old .part file stoppedThis is only necessary if a "one-time" download link gets interrupted part-way through, eg. by a flaky connection. Attempting to resume a one-time link like normal gets (I assume) a 400 response and FF kills the .part file.
Who remembers Getright?https://www.getright.com/

Resumable downloads in firefox generally appear to be fairly unstable though. This has been a known problem in some form since as far back as 2005.It's odd how the experience differs so much; I clearly remember successfully resuming a download less than a month ago, and I don't remember any time Firefox had any problems with them. My network.http.response.timeout is the default of 300.There are reasons, but until someone actually publishes an article that's more detailed than the vagueness here, there's nothing anyone can really do about it.
